title: Neurogenesis How To Grow New Brain Cells Naturally
header: Unlock the science behind how your brain can still create new neurons
content:
Can Adults Grow New Neurons?

For many years, scientists believed adults could not grow new brain cells. New research from the Karolinska Institutet in Sweden shows that adult brains can naturally make new neurons. This process may help with conditions like Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, ALS, MND, TBI, and stroke.

Adults make about 700–1000 new neurons per day. These new cells form mainly in the hippocampus, subventricular zone, and dentate gyrus — areas important for memory and learning.

What Is Neurogenesis?

Neurogenesis means the creation of new neurons in the brain. Here are the key points:

  1. Adults can grow new neurons: This mostly happens in the hippocampus, helping learning and memory.
  2. Neural stem cells: These special cells can create new neurons and help repair brain tissue.
  3. Medical research: Growing stem cells in labs helps scientists study diseases and explore new treatments.
  4. Brain organoids: 3D “mini brains” made from stem cells help scientists study disorders and test therapies.
  5. Clinical challenges: Turning lab discoveries into safe treatments for humans is still difficult.
  6. History: Early scientists like Joseph Altman suggested adult neurogenesis long ago, but it took years to be accepted.
  7. New technology: Modern imaging and cell-growth methods allow deeper study of brain development and disease.
  8. Ethical issues: Stem cell sources, cost, and large-scale production remain challenges for real-world therapies.

New Brain Cells Across a Lifetime

Humans are born with almost 100 billion neurons. After age 3, neurogenesis slows down everywhere except the hippocampus. Scientists believe evolution may have chosen stability over constant regeneration.

How to Boost Adult Neurogenesis Naturally

Some lifestyle habits may support the growth of new brain cells:

  • Intermittent fasting or eating slightly fewer calories
  • Flavonoids (blueberries, dark chocolate)
  • Omega-3 fats (salmon and other fatty fish)
  • Aerobic and cardio exercise

Habits That Reduce Neurogenesis

  • Diets high in sugar and saturated fat
  • Frequent alcohol use
  • Lack of exercise
  • Vitamin A, B, or D deficiency
  • Chronic stress, poor sleep, and normal aging

In the future, understanding neurogenesis may help create therapies that repair the brain or improve quality of life as we age.

title: Simple Steps to Start Loving and Valuing Yourself
header: Explore gentle mindset shifts that help you finally put yourself first
content:
It’s time to prioritize your happiness and well-being. These simple steps can help you love and value yourself more.

Self-love and self-care are essential for a healthy, fulfilling life. Many people forget to put themselves first, but you can change that with small daily actions.

Practice Self-Care Daily

Take time each day to do something that makes you feel good. It can be a warm bath, a walk outside, deep breathing, or a few minutes of meditation. Caring for yourself builds confidence and reminds you that you deserve love and respect.

Surround Yourself with Positive People

The people around you influence your self-esteem. Spend time with those who support, encourage, and uplift you. Limit time with people who are negative, critical, or draining. You deserve healthy, positive relationships.

Stop Comparing Yourself to Others

Comparison is one of the biggest barriers to self-love. Everyone has struggles you may not see. Focus on your own growth and celebrate your wins. You are unique, and your journey is your own.

Forgive Yourself for Past Mistakes

Everyone makes mistakes. They do not define you. Learn from them and move forward. Self-forgiveness takes time, but it helps you grow and feel lighter.

Set Boundaries and Say No

Saying no is an important part of valuing yourself. Protect your time, energy, and mental health. Set limits with toxic people, avoid draining events, and decline tasks that don’t support your goals. Saying no is self-respect.

title: Smiling Is Contagious
header: Learn why one smile can change how you feel—and how others feel too
content:
“Whenever I see your smiling face, I have to smile myself,” sang James Taylor — and he was right. Smiling is contagious. It is free, easy, and has powerful benefits for both you and others.

A smile is unique. It costs nothing, yet it has great value. It is one of the first ways humans communicate. Smiles are instinctive, not learned. They are also very recognizable — people can identify someone by their smile from far away.

Not All Smiles Are the Same

The most sincere smile is the Duchenne smile. It happens when the corners of the mouth lift and the eyes crinkle into “crow’s feet.” This is the smile that shows true happiness. Model Tyra Banks later called this “smizing” — smiling with your eyes.

How Smiling Helps You

Smiling has “superpowers.” It can make you look younger, more attractive, and more confident. It helps you appear friendly and approachable.

Smiling also boosts your mood. It releases dopamine, endorphins, and serotonin — chemicals that make you feel happy and relaxed. Even a “fake” smile can trick your brain into feeling better.

Smiling may reduce stress, lower blood pressure, support your immune system, and even help you live longer.

How Smiling Helps Others

A smile is a universal sign of kindness. When you smile at someone, they feel calmer, welcomed, and more connected to you. Your smile also triggers their “feel-good” chemicals — happiness spreads quickly.

Even seeing someone else smile can uplift your mood. That’s why it’s helpful to smile more often.

Thanking the Smiling Eyes at Monarch Landing

During recent years, the staff at Monarch Landing and The Springs Health and Rehabilitation Center continued to care for residents with dedication — and warm “smizing” eyes, even behind masks.

Residents noticed and appreciated this kindness. Since employees cannot accept personal gifts, the annual Staff Appreciation Fund allows residents to express gratitude to the caring team who kept them safe, healthy, and supported.

title: The Power of Intermittent Fasting
header: Learn why intermittent fasting can improve health, habits, and even savings
content:
Intermittent fasting (IF) may feel challenging at first, but with practice your body adjusts. Many people try IF for weight loss, better sleep, lower blood pressure, improved insulin sensitivity, and even long-term health benefits.

A 2019 study in The New England Journal of Medicine linked intermittent fasting to better stress resistance, longer lifespan, and a lower risk of diseases like cancer and obesity.

What is intermittent fasting?

Most people eat for 13 hours or more each day. Intermittent fasting simply means shortening your eating window. For example, you might eat between 12 p.m. and 8 p.m. (16:8 method). You are not denying yourself food — you are only delaying it.

IF works best when you keep a “clean” fast (no calories during fasting hours). Once your body adjusts, your hunger becomes easier to manage.

Why many people like intermittent fasting

IF is simple and free. You don’t need books, gadgets, supplements, or special foods. You just change your eating schedule.

Unlike diets such as keto, paleo, Atkins, or others, IF does not ban food groups. You can still enjoy your favorite foods during your eating window — just in reasonable portions.

“Delay, don’t deny” mindset

Author Gin Stephens explains that IF becomes easier over time. Diets usually get harder the longer you follow them. IF is the opposite — it gets easier as your body adapts.

Hidden benefit: saving money

Eating fewer meals often means spending less money. For example, if you normally spend $100 a week on food, cutting out daily breakfasts and snacks might lower it to $70.

Saving $30 per week adds up to around $120 per month or $1,440 per year — enough for a trip or a down payment.

Eating less can also lower your environmental impact by reducing food waste and resource use.

Before trying intermittent fasting, always check with a doctor, especially if you have medical conditions or take medication.

title: We are happier when we're busy, even if it's pointless work
header: Discover why staying busy makes people happier than doing nothing
content:
Would you rather do nothing or do something that serves no real purpose? Research shows most people choose doing something over doing nothing — and they feel happier when they stay busy.

In a University of Chicago study, students could walk 15 minutes to drop off a questionnaire or drop it right outside the room and wait. Both choices earned the same candy. When the candy was the same, 68% chose the easy option. But when different candies were offered, 59% chose the longer walk — even though both candies were equally liked.

The simple promise of “something different” made people choose busyness. Afterward, students who walked reported being happier than those who waited. Even when they were forced to walk or forced to wait, people were still happier when they were kept busy.

Why does this happen? Researchers believe it may be tied to evolution. Long ago, humans had to save energy to survive, so we avoided unnecessary activity. Today, we have more energy and fewer survival risks, so we prefer to release that energy by staying active. Our instinct pushes us toward rest, but our minds feel better when we are busy.

Businesses use this insight. Some airports increased the walking distance from the gate to baggage carousels. Passengers don’t get their bags faster, but they complain less because they stay busy walking instead of waiting.

We do this in daily life too. Many people take longer driving routes just to avoid sitting in traffic because movement feels better than waiting.

Something to think about: At work, are you busy because the task matters — or because being busy simply feels better than being idle?

title: How Does Mental Health Affect Physical Health?
header: Unlock the powerful link between your mind, body, and overall health
content:
The mind and body are closely connected. Good mental health can improve physical health, and poor mental health can harm it.

Effects of Mental Health on Physical Health

Your mental health strongly affects your overall well-being. Positive mental health can lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Poor mental health can lead to harmful habits or worsen physical conditions.

Chronic diseases. Depression is linked to diabetes, asthma, cancer, cardiovascular disease, and arthritis. Schizophrenia also raises the risk of heart and lung diseases. Mental health issues can make managing chronic illnesses harder.

Sleep problems. Mental health conditions often come with insomnia or sleep apnea. Around 50–80% of people with mental health issues have sleep problems, compared to about 10–18% of the general population. Poor sleep can worsen mental health further.

Smoking. People with mental health conditions are more likely to smoke and smoke more often. Nicotine briefly boosts dopamine, making smoking feel relieving—but this can lead to addiction.

Access to health care. Many people with mental health conditions struggle to access or manage medical care. It may feel hard to seek help, take medication regularly, or stay active.

Physical Health Conditions That Affect Mental Health

Physical illnesses can also impact mental health.

Psoriasis. This skin condition causes painful sores and is linked to stress and depression due to stigma and emotional distress.

Serious illnesses like cancer or heart attacks can also lead to depression or anxiety. About one-third of people with major medical conditions experience low mood, sleep problems, or loss of interest.

How to Care for Both Your Mental and Physical Health

  • Get regular exercise. Even a daily 10-minute walk can boost energy and mood.
  • Eat a balanced diet. More fruits and vegetables and fewer processed foods can improve mental and physical well-being.
  • Avoid alcohol and drugs. These may offer short-term relief but can harm long-term health.
  • Get enough sleep. Aim for 7–9 hours each night. A short daytime nap can also help.
  • Try relaxation techniques. Meditation and deep breathing can reduce stress.
  • Practice positive thinking. Try to focus on positive events and emotions.
  • Seek support. Talking with friends or family can reduce stress and help you cope.

title: How much energy do we expend using our brains?
header: Find out why your brain feels tired even when energy use barely changes
content:
After a long day of work or study, your brain may feel drained. But does thinking hard actually use more energy than doing something easy, like watching TV?

The brain runs on a molecule called ATP, made from sugar and oxygen. Even though the brain is only 2% of our body weight, it uses about 20% of our daily energy. That’s around 260 calories a day.

How do we know this?

Studies show that about 75% of the brain’s energy is used for processing information — sending signals, thinking, and reacting. The remaining 25% is used for basic cell maintenance.

Scientists can’t measure this directly in humans, but they can track oxygen use. When the brain works harder, it needs more oxygen, and this change can be measured through CO₂ levels or MRI scans.

Can we measure brain oxygen use exactly?

Not perfectly. MRI can show which parts of the brain become more active, but it only shows relative changes — not exactly how much energy each task uses. That’s because the brain is always active, even when we feel relaxed.

Even when resting, we process sounds, sights, memories, plans, and emotions — all of which use energy.

How much does brain activity increase?

Surprisingly little. For example, paying close attention to a moving object increases activity in the visual cortex by only about 1%. And when one area becomes more active, another area (like the auditory system) may reduce activity, balancing total brain energy use.

So why do we feel mentally exhausted?

The tired feeling usually comes from stress, not energy shortage. Hard mental tasks activate the body’s stress system, which can make us feel mentally and physically tired.

The good news: Thinking hard won’t drain your brain’s energy reserves. But taking breaks helps prevent stress and overload.
author: Dr Oliver Baumann.

title: Vegetarian Snacks To Stay Full And Energetic
header: Discover easy vegetarian snacks that keep you full and energized
content:
Snacking is an important part of a healthy diet. But quick, easy snacks are often high in sugar, salt, and empty calories. Choosing the right snacks can help you stay full, energized, and on track. Here are simple vegetarian snacks that are portable, nutritious, and easy to prepare.

1. Apple with peanut butter

Apples are rich in fibre and help control hunger. Paired with peanut butter, this snack gives you healthy fats, protein, vitamin E, and potassium.

2. Roasted chana

title: Iron-Deficiency Symptoms and How to Eat More of the Mineral
header: Explore the common symptoms of low iron most people ignore
content:
Feeling tired or weak all the time? You might not be getting enough iron. Iron helps your body make red blood cells that carry oxygen. Low iron can cause anemia and many everyday symptoms.

How much iron do you need?

Men need 8 mg per day. Women need 18 mg per day (8 mg after age 51). Pregnant women need 27 mg, and breastfeeding women need 9 mg daily.

Foods rich in iron

  • Red meat, poultry, pork
  • Beans and peas
  • Seafood
  • Dark leafy greens (spinach, kale)
  • Dried fruits (raisins, apricots)
  • Nuts
  • Iron-fortified cereals and pasta

Who is at higher risk?

People who menstruate, infants, kids in growth spurts, frequent blood donors, vegans/vegetarians, and anyone with poor absorption or certain medical issues.

Common signs of iron deficiency

• Extreme tiredness or weakness

Low iron means less oxygen reaches your body, making you feel tired and drained.

• Chest discomfort or fast heartbeat

Your heart works harder when your blood carries less oxygen.

• Headaches, dizziness, lightheadedness

Low oxygen to the brain can lead to headaches and trouble focusing.

• Cold hands and feet

Poor oxygen flow can make your extremities feel cold.

• Cravings for non-food items

Pica (craving ice, soil, paper) can appear in severe iron deficiency.

• Poor appetite

Some people lose hunger due to changes in hormones and blood proteins.

• Pale skin

Fewer red blood cells can make skin look lighter or washed out.

What causes iron deficiency?

Not eating enough iron, heavy bleeding, pregnancy, poor absorption, stomach issues, certain illnesses, or frequent blood donation.

How to add more iron to your diet

  • Cook in cast-iron pans
  • Choose iron-rich recipes and snacks
  • Eat nuts, seeds, whole grains
  • Pair iron foods with vitamin C to improve absorption
  • Pick iron-fortified cereals or breads
  • Add spinach, peas, lentils or mushrooms to salads

If symptoms appear, ask your doctor for a blood test. Supplements can help, but only take them with medical advice.

title: Does Birth Order Really Determine Personality? Here’s What the Research Says
header: Learn what truly influences personality beyond birth order
content:
Many people believe firstborns and later-born children have different personalities. But does birth order truly shape who we become? The idea has been debated for more than 100 years, and research shows the truth is far more complicated.

Where birth-order beliefs began

In 1874, Francis Galton noticed that many famous scientists were firstborns. Later, Alfred Adler suggested firstborns become responsible and anxious, middle children become peacemakers, and youngest children become more carefree. These ideas became popular and shaped how parents viewed their kids.

Why the theory spread

Older generations practiced primogeniture, meaning the oldest child—usually the son—got more attention, education, and inheritance. Naturally, this created differences between siblings, and people assumed personality was the reason.

Modern research tells a different story

Recent studies with hundreds of thousands of people found:

  • Birth order has tiny or no real effect on personality.
  • Any differences are so small they are not meaningful.
  • Older children may score slightly higher on IQ tests, likely because parents can give the first child more one-on-one attention early in life.

Overall, personality differences usually come from age, environment, family roles, and expectations—not birth order itself.

Why it still feels real

We often confuse birth order with age. Older kids naturally act more mature, and younger kids express emotions more openly. Parents also assign roles like “responsible older one” or “easygoing younger one,” which influence behavior.

Because these patterns feel familiar, people continue to believe birth order shapes personality—even when science says the effect is tiny.

The takeaway

Your child—or you—are not defined by being firstborn, middle, or youngest. Personality comes from many factors: experiences, environment, family dynamics, and personal growth.

Birth-order stories are comforting and fun, but they’re not destiny. Our personalities are shaped far more by how we are raised and how we grow—not the order in which we are born.

title: Why we need other people to be happy

Humans are built for connection. Being lonely can harm both physical and emotional health, while strong social ties can make us happier and healthier.

1. Being around people makes us healthier

Loneliness raises stress hormones like cortisol. Chronic stress can increase the risk of heart disease, cancer and a weaker immune system. Studies show people with fewer social ties have higher illness rates and even shorter lifespans. Strong relationships help us stay healthy and recover better.

2. Our brains work better together

Research shows the brain functions more efficiently during real social interaction. Talking with someone is easier for the brain than listening to long monologues. Children also learn better through interaction than through simple observation.

3. We are wired to belong

Humans naturally prefer doing life with others. The “need to belong” theory suggests we instinctively form social bonds and try to maintain them. Social baseline theory says our brains expect relationships because being with others makes challenges feel smaller and life feel safer.

Experiments show that holding someone’s hand reduces fear, and standing with a friend can make a steep hill look easier. Simply having someone we trust nearby changes how we see the world.

4. Difficult people can help us grow

Even the people who annoy us can help us learn and expand our perspective. Feeling irritated, sad or anxious sometimes increases our ability to feel joy later. Growth often happens in challenging relationships—as long as the relationship isn’t harmful or draining.

Be grateful for your people

Practicing gratitude strengthens relationships and boosts happiness. People who express gratitude tend to feel better, handle stress more easily and enjoy deeper connections.

Take time to notice who adds goodness to your life and say “thank you.” And remember: alone time is healthy too. Rest and reflection help you return to your social world with more energy and clarity.

title: How Human Memory Works
header: Unlock How Your Memory Really Works and Why You Forget Simple Things
content:
Short and Long Term Memory

Our memory works in stages. First comes sensory memory, then short-term memory, and finally long-term memory. These stages help filter the huge amount of information we experience every day.

Memory starts with perception. Sensory memory holds sights, sounds, or touches for a brief moment. After this, the information moves to short-term memory, which holds about 7 items for 20–30 seconds. Techniques like repeating or “chunking” can help you hold information longer.

With repetition or use, information can move into long-term memory. Long-term memory has a very large capacity and can store information for years. We remember things more easily when they connect to something we already know.

Memory Retrieval

To remember something, your brain retrieves stored information and brings it into your conscious mind. Memory struggles usually happen because one part of the system (encoding, storage, or retrieval) didn’t work well — not because your entire memory is “bad.”

Example: remembering where you left your eyeglasses. You must pay attention when placing them (encoding), hold the information (storage), and recall it later (retrieval). If one step fails, you may “forget.”

Why forgetting happens:

  • You didn’t encode the information clearly.
  • You didn’t retain it long enough.
  • You’re having trouble retrieving it.

Distractions can block encoding — for example, reading in a noisy place makes it harder for your brain to store information properly. Sometimes retrieval cues don’t match how the memory was stored, so you remember later even if you couldn’t recall it earlier.

Memory challenges also increase with age, but improving attention, reducing distractions, and strengthening retrieval cues can help.

title: Extroverts enjoy four key advantages according to science
header: Unlock the Hidden Workplace Advantages Extroverts Tend to Have
content:
Why Extroverts May Have Workplace Advantages

A new University of Toronto review of 91 meta-analyses looked at how extroversion relates to 165 work-related traits (motivation, well-being, performance, etc.). The research finds a small but consistent advantage for extroverted people at work, especially in four areas.

Who is an extrovert?

Typical extrovert traits: talkative, outgoing, takes charge, open to new experiences, shows positive emotion. Introverts are quieter, more reserved, and less energetic.

Four clear advantages for extroverts

  • Motivation: Extroverts tend to be more driven to pursue positive goals at work.
  • Positive emotion: They experience positive feelings more often, which boosts satisfaction and buffers stress.
  • Interpersonal skills: Better social skills, communication, and persuasion help them in teamwork and leadership.
  • Job performance: Extroverts often score better on job performance — likely because motivation, mood, and social skill combine over time.

What this means for introverts

The study does not mean introverts are doomed. Most people show a mix of introverted and extroverted behaviors. Other traits (intelligence, conscientiousness, emotion regulation) strongly affect success too. Many jobs favour introverted strengths (e.g., focused programming, deep analysis).

Limitations & takeaways

  • This review focused only on extroversion and work variables — many other factors matter for success.
  • Advantages are generally small and cumulative — they grow across a career rather than instantly turning someone into a top performer.
  • If you’re introverted, leverage your strengths (focus, listening, depth) and cultivate social, motivational, or emotional skills where helpful.

Bottom line: Extroversion gives small, reliable workplace advantages in motivation, mood, social skill, and performance — but it is only one of many ingredients that predict success.

title: Why you should spend money on experiences, not stuff

content:
Why You Should Spend Money on Experiences, Not Things

We work hard for our money, and naturally we want to use it in ways that bring joy. But research from universities like Cornell shows that the happiness we get from buying “things” fades quickly. Experiences, on the other hand, stay with us much longer.

Why buying things doesn’t make us happy for long

New items feel exciting at first, but the joy fades fast. We adapt, the item becomes normal, and the happiness “depreciates” — just like a new car losing value the moment it leaves the lot.

The “bigger and better” cycle

Once we get used to one item, we start wanting the next one. We compare ourselves to others, try to keep up, and end up chasing upgrades that never truly satisfy.

Why experiences are more powerful

  • Experiences shape identity: We remember what we’ve done, not what we owned. Memories, moments, and adventures become part of who we are.
  • Anticipation feels amazing: Planning and looking forward to an experience creates happiness long before it even happens.
  • Less comparison: It’s easy to compare items, but it’s harder to compare personal experiences — they’re unique and meaningful.
  • The time paradox: Experiences may be short, but their impact lasts for years. Even difficult moments can become important life stories.

Experiences grow in value

Unlike objects that lose their excitement, experiences often become more meaningful over time. We remember the joy, the growth, the people we met, and the way we felt.

The bottom line

Buy what you need and enjoy what you love — but when it comes to creating lasting happiness, experiences give far more value than things. They stay with you, shape you, and become the stories you carry through life.

title: Difference between short and long term memory?
header: Discover the Key Difference Between Short Term and Long Term Memory Loss
content:
Short Term vs Long Term Memory Loss

Short term and long term memory work differently, and understanding the difference helps explain dementia symptoms.

In a nutshell

Your brain processes thousands of thoughts and experiences every day. Some stay in your mind for seconds or minutes, some for days, and others for years or a lifetime. These stored thoughts form your memories, which fall into short term memory or long term memory.

What is short term memory?

Short term memory holds recent information, like what you ate for breakfast or the show you watched last night. These memories last from about 30 seconds to a few days and are often forgotten to make room for new information.

Some short term memories move into long term memory when we focus on them or intentionally try to remember them. This process happens in the brain’s frontal lobe.

What is long term memory?

Long term memory stores events, facts and experiences from weeks, months or years ago. When you decide something is important to remember, your brain strengthens connections between cells, helping the memory stay.

Some memories, like childhood fun or sad events, stay long term because they are tied to strong emotions or sensory experiences.

Good to know

Long term memory includes different types such as:
- Declarative memory (facts)
- Procedural memory (skills like tying shoelaces)

Memory loss in dementia

People with dementia often remember events from long ago but struggle to recall recent events. This is because diseases like Alzheimer’s affect short term memory first. Long term memories may fade later as the disease progresses.

When to get help

If you notice ongoing short term memory problems, see a doctor early. A proper assessment can show how serious the issue is and what support or treatment may help.

title: How Long Do Dreams Last?
header: Find Out What Science Reveals About Dream Length and Time
content:
Dreams have fascinated people for centuries. They can make us feel wonder, joy, confusion, or inspiration. Modern science has uncovered a lot about dreams, but there is still much we don’t fully understand.

How long do we dream each night?

The average person dreams for about two hours each night. Early REM sleep lasts around 10 minutes and gets longer through the night, sometimes up to one hour. But dream length is hard to measure because not all dreams happen in REM sleep, and people often forget their dreams.

Some studies show that dream time may match real time. Lucid dreamers can sometimes signal time inside a dream with eye movements, helping researchers estimate dream length.

Bizarre dreams may feel longer than they are, and lucid dreamers often take longer to perform tasks in dreams than in real life.

Why do dreams seem long?

One idea is that brain activity slows down during REM sleep, making dream events feel slower. Another theory says that since our muscles are paralyzed in REM sleep, the brain “pretends” certain actions take more effort, making them feel longer.

What affects dream length?

REM dreams are usually longer, more emotional, and more story-like. NREM dreams tend to be shorter and more like scattered thoughts.

Dreams later in the night are usually more detailed. Studies show that after 10 minutes of REM sleep later in the night, people reported longer and more complex dreams.

How many dreams do we have?

We dream in all stages of sleep. A full sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes, and most people go through four to six cycles a night. That means multiple dream periods, especially toward morning when REM sleep increases.

Does everyone dream?

Almost everyone dreams, even if they don’t remember. Some people think they never dream, but this is often due to poor dream recall. Damage to certain brain areas can make dreaming difficult.

Children’s dreams develop as their memory grows. Older adults often have less REM sleep and may remember fewer dreams. People who are blind may dream with more sounds, smells, and touch instead of visuals.

How to remember your dreams

Keeping a dream journal can improve dream recall. Write down or record your dreams as soon as you wake up. Since the brain forms fewer memories during sleep, waking up briefly can help a dream move into long-term memory.

2. Exercise regularly

Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week. Activities like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming support heart health.

3. Avoid smoking and limit alcohol

Smoking and heavy drinking raise heart attack risk. Quitting smoking and drinking in moderation can greatly improve heart health.

4. Manage stress

5. Get regular check-ups

6. Maintain a healthy weight

7. Control diabetes

Diabetes greatly increases heart risk. Managing blood sugar with diet, exercise, and medication (if needed) is essential.

8. Get enough sleep

Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep. Poor sleep can raise blood pressure and increase heart disease risk.

9. Limit red and processed meats

These foods are high in saturated fat. Choose lean meats, fish, beans, and plant proteins instead.

10. Practice good oral hygiene

Poor gum health is linked to heart disease. Brush, floss, and visit your dentist regularly.

Small, consistent lifestyle changes—like meal planning, scheduled workouts, better sleep habits, or support from friends and healthcare providers—can make a big difference over time.

title: How Do You Define Your Self-Worth?
header: Learn How to Stop Burning Yourself Out for Others
content:
"You are not required to set yourself on fire to keep other people warm." This quote speaks to anyone who gives too much. Many of us try to carry others' problems, please everyone, and lose ourselves in the process.

Learning to measure your own value

We grow up believing our value depends on what we do for others. As kids we try to make parents proud. As teens we try to fit in. As adults we try to be loved. Soon our self-worth feels tied to pleasing people and being "good enough."

When we stop doing things for others, our self-worth drops. If someone is disappointed in us, it crashes.

Giving too much doesn’t make you more lovable

For years, I tried to be useful so people would like me. I paid bills for others, bought gifts, lent money, and gave my time even when I was drained. I thought kindness would make people value me. Instead, it left me empty.

Some people appreciated it. Many took advantage. I kept giving more, hoping it would finally make me feel worthy.

Why boundaries change everything

Eventually, my emotional and financial energy ran out. I realized my worth did not come from giving nonstop. I learned to set boundaries and say no. I learned that healthy relationships give both ways, not just one way.

You are allowed to protect your energy. You are allowed to decide who deserves your help. You are allowed to step back.

Building your life raises your self-worth

My value grew when I focused on my own life—hobbies, routine, joy, health, quiet moments, and people who respected me. When I stopped trying to prove I was a "good person," I finally felt like one.

I had more energy to give in healthy ways, not to earn approval but because I was full, not empty.

A reminder you might need today

You are worth more than what you give others. You do not need to give until nothing is left. Choose people who respect your boundaries and give back to you. Turn some of your kindness toward yourself and see how good it feels.

title: Why Are Extraverts More Satisfied? Personality, Social Experiences, and Subjective Well–Being in College
header: Learn What Science Says About Extraversion and Life Satisfaction
content:
Extraversion is well known to be linked with higher happiness and life satisfaction. But the reason behind this connection is not fully clear.

Two long-term studies followed college students for 4 years to explore whether extraversion improves well-being by shaping social experiences. In both studies, students who were more extraverted at the start of college reported higher well-being 4 years later.

Extraverted students also reported better social experiences, such as feeling a stronger sense of belonging and having larger social networks. Both self-reports and peer-reports supported this pattern.

The researchers tested whether either the quality or quantity of social experiences explained why extraverts became happier. In the first study, neither factor fully explained the effect. In the second study, only the quality of social experiences—such as meaningful connections—helped explain the higher well-being.

Overall, the findings suggest that extraverts may feel happier partly because they create better social experiences. However, social life is not the only reason extraverts show greater satisfaction. Other factors also contribute to their well-being.

title: Negative people are making us sick, but here’s what can we do
header: Learn How to Break Free From Negative People Without Guilt
content:
Just like we can catch physical toxins, we can also catch other people’s negativity. Research shows that negativity can affect both our mental and physical health.

“Let’s set ourselves free from the tethers of negative people and give ourselves the opportunity to navigate our own lives.”

Negative people can affect our mood and mind

Being around negativity for a long time can slowly change how our brain works. It can make us more anxious, more stressed, and more pessimistic. Over time, this rewiring can raise the risk of depression, heart problems, and a weaker immune system.

Why negativity spreads

Humans naturally copy the behaviour of their social group. Our brains reward us when we fit in and agree with others. This is an old survival mechanism from our ancestors. Because of this, being around negative people can slowly make us think and act like them without noticing.

How negativity rewires the brain

Our brains release a small reward (dopamine) when we match the opinions or moods of others. This makes it easier over time for negative thinking to become our “default mode.” Once these patterns form, reversing them takes effort, because the brain prefers the easiest, most familiar pathway.

Why some people pull others down

People with low self-esteem or negative self-beliefs may drag others down to feel less threatened. This can be intentional or unconscious, but the result is the same—they keep everyone at their level to protect their ego.

Negativity harms physical health too

Negative emotions don’t just affect the mind. Studies show they can harm memory, reasoning, and even increase the risk of heart attack or stroke. New research also shows that negative emotions weaken the immune system, making us more vulnerable to illness.

How to protect yourself from negative people

1. Lessen your exposure

You may not be able to cut someone out completely, but you can reduce how often you see or speak to them.

2. Strengthen your sense of self

Knowing your values and who you are makes it easier to ignore unfair criticism or negativity directed at you.

3. Understand their negativity

Negative people often project their own fears and insecurities onto others. Realising this can help you detach emotionally.

4. Remember that positivity spreads too

Your happiness, gratitude, and resilience can influence others. You don’t have to “fix” them—you just model a different way of thinking.

5. Encourage gratitude

Many unhappy people focus on what they lack. Sharing your gratitude habits may help them shift their perspective.

6. Suggest help when needed

If someone close to you is struggling and aware of it, gently guide them toward getting professional support.

7. Stop giving negative people your energy

We often replay negative interactions in our minds. Instead, choose where to place your mental focus. Invest your energy in thoughts that help you grow.

Give yourself permission to step free

Negative people are not “bad,” but their influence can be harmful. We owe it to ourselves to protect our mental and physical well-being. Reducing exposure, keeping strong boundaries, and building self-worth can set us free to explore our potential and live a happier life.

title: Why Some People Always Remember Their Dreams and Others Forget
header: Unlock the Science Behind Remembering and Forgetting Dreams
content:
Since childhood, I’ve been able to remember my dreams almost every day. Some fade quickly, but others stay in my mind for months or years. I used to believe everyone remembered their dreams too, until I learned in high school that most people don’t.

Why we dream

Dreams usually happen during REM sleep. This sleep stage begins about 90 minutes after falling asleep and becomes longer toward morning. During REM sleep, the brain is very active, which is why dreams feel vivid.

Experts agree that everyone dreams, whether they remember it or not. Dreaming is a normal part of brain function, but researchers still debate exactly why dreams happen.

Why we remember (or forget) dreams

Some scientists believe dreams occur while the brain processes information, clears out unnecessary details, and stores important memories. This may explain why some people naturally recall dreams more easily than others.

In some cases, the brain may intentionally block dream memories. If a dream feels too real or intense, forgetting it helps us separate dream life from real life.

Other times, brain activity can make dreams easier to remember. A region called the temporoparietal junction helps process emotions and may help the brain “wake up” slightly during sleep, allowing dream memories to form.

Why some people remember more dreams

Lack of sleep can reduce REM sleep, making dream recall harder. Personality also plays a role. People who daydream, think creatively, or spend time in deep thought tend to remember dreams more often. More practical or externally focused people may recall fewer dreams.

Stress, trauma, or grief can also create vivid dreams or nightmares that are easier to remember the next day.

Does dreaming affect sleep quality?

Dreaming itself does not harm sleep. But remembering dreams more often may be linked to frequent awakenings caused by alarms, irregular sleep schedules, sleep apnea, alcohol, or other sleep disruptions.

If vivid dreams or nightmares wake you up often, or you feel very tired during the day, it may be helpful to speak with a doctor. This is especially important for people experiencing trauma-related nightmares.

The bottom line

Researchers still have much to learn about dreaming, but remembering dreams is completely normal. It doesn’t mean you aren’t sleeping well, and it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Some dreams may even inspire creativity or storytelling — even if they involve a week of dreaming about snakes!

title: How Stress Can Affect Your Memory?
header: Explore the Hidden Link Between Stress and Memory Loss
content:
A little stress can help you stay alert and motivated. But too much stress can harm your physical health, mental health, emotions, relationships — and your memory. High, ongoing stress can interfere with how your brain stores and recalls information.

Short-term stress can support memory

Moderate, brief stress (like before a quiz) can help learning. When stressed in small amounts, the body releases cortisol. This signals the amygdala to tell the hippocampus to save the new information. This helps the brain acquire, consolidate, and encode memories.

How intense stress harms memory

Memory encoding

When stress is very high, your brain focuses on the stress reaction. It becomes harder to encode new information, so it never moves into long-term memory.

Memory recall

If you feel highly stressed during a test, you may struggle to retrieve information that you normally remember.

How chronic stress affects the brain

Memory takes a back seat

Chronic stress keeps the brain in constant “survival mode.” This reduces energy available for long-term memory and higher thinking. Encoding and recall both suffer.

Long-term brain changes

Research shows that ongoing stress increases activity in primitive survival areas of the brain and decreases activity in areas responsible for memory and complex thinking. Over time, chronic stress can even shrink the hippocampus, which supports memory.

Managing stress to protect memory

Managing stress helps improve brain function and memory. Start by noticing your main stress triggers and how your body and mind react to stress. Then use simple strategies to gain control.

  • Create a predictable daily routine
  • Get enough sleep every night
  • Exercise daily, even light activity
  • Ask for help when needed
  • Organize a manageable workload

You need some stress to learn and grow — but you don’t need chronic stress that overwhelms your brain and harms your health.

Why experiences are better than things

  • Memory & anticipation: Experiences give joy before, during, and after they happen.
  • Identity & connection: Experiences become part of your story and help build stronger relationships.
  • Less comparison: It’s easier to compare objects than experiences, so experiences create less envy.

What research shows

  • People report more happiness from experiences at every stage — before, during, and after.
  • “Hybrid” purchases (like a smartwatch or camper) also feel rewarding because they create experiences.

How to apply this

  • Pick a concert over a new gadget.
  • Choose a weekend trip instead of new clothes.
  • Try a cooking class rather than buying another item.

Think of it as investing in memories, growth, and moments that stay with you — not just things that sit on a shelf.

title: What is Gratitude and Why Is It So Important?
header: Find Out Why Gratitude Is One of the Most Powerful Mindset Tools
content:
When you feel low or stuck, how do you cope? Many people turn to food, shopping, or other quick fixes. But one powerful, free tool to lift your mood is gratitude.

Gratitude turns what you have into enough.
Gratitude is more than saying thank you.
Gratitude changes how you see your world.

If finding the positive feels hard, you’re not alone. Gratitude helps you notice small moments of good even during tough times. Here’s what gratitude means, why it matters, and how to practice it daily.

What Gratitude Really Means

Gratitude is the feeling of thankfulness and appreciation. It can be a momentary emotion or a lasting personal habit.

Gratitude has two simple parts:

  • Acknowledging the good in your life.
  • Recognizing that some of this good comes from outside yourself.

Gratitude can be a trait you develop over time or a feeling you experience when someone shows kindness.

Gratitude in Positive Psychology

In positive psychology, gratitude is a core emotion linked to happiness, hope, resilience, and stronger relationships. Research consistently shows that practicing gratitude increases overall wellbeing.

Why Gratitude Matters

In modern life, many comforts are taken for granted. Gratitude helps reverse this by shifting focus back to appreciation. Benefits include:

  • Improved mood and life satisfaction
  • Better relationships
  • More empathy and kindness
  • Lower stress, anxiety, and depression

Gratitude often inspires a ripple effect—when you feel grateful, you’re more likely to help others, and people who are appreciated are more likely to help in return.

Gratitude Across Cultures

Many traditions include gratitude as a core value:

  • Buddhism: Gratitude for the interconnected nature of life.
  • Judaism: Morning prayers expressing thanks for a new day.
  • Christianity: Blessings and prayers of gratitude for life and daily gifts.

The Role of Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is a yearly reminder to pause and appreciate what we have. But gratitude doesn’t require a holiday—it’s a mindset we can practice every day.

How to Show Gratitude

Gratitude can be simple, heartfelt, and personal. Try expressing it through thoughtful words, journaling, or small acts of kindness.

When saying thank you, focus on two things: how you feel and the effort someone made. For example:

“Your gift made my day. I appreciate the time you took to find something so meaningful for me.”

“Mom, thank you for everything you’ve done. I’m grateful for your love, hard work, and sacrifices.”

“I’m grateful for my health, my senses, and another day of life.”

“Feeling gratitude and not expressing it is like wrapping a present and not giving it.” — William Arthur Ward

Don’t try to control the uncontrollable. Focus on what you can control—your actions and your reactions—instead of the behavior of others or situations outside your power.

Look for the upside. Difficult moments can teach you important lessons and help you grow. If your choices played a role in the stress, reflect and learn from them.

Learn to forgive. No one is perfect. Letting go of anger and resentment frees your mind and reduces stress.

Share your feelings. Talking to someone you trust—or a therapist—can help you feel lighter, even if the situation cannot be changed.

7. Follow your heart

Your passions give life meaning. Listen to what inspires you and take small steps toward the things that light you up.

Everything begins with how you treat yourself. When you value who you are, your relationships and your life reflect that love outward.

title: Smiling can trick your brain into happiness — and boost your health

Fake It Till You Make It

Smiling can also improve social interactions. A simple smile can warm up a conversation, help you connect with strangers, and make travel or daily life feel smoother.

How Smiling Goes Viral

Smiling is contagious. Mirror neurons in the brain make us copy the expressions we see, so when someone smiles at you, you naturally want to smile back. A genuine smile also sends “good vibes,” which encourages others to pass it on.

You can even catch a smile from yourself. Smiling at your reflection can reduce anxiety and help you re-center when you’re feeling stressed.

Simple smile experiments — like smiling in traffic or during a tough workout — show that smiling in tense moments can help you feel calmer almost instantly.

Smiling is a small action with big benefits. Use it as a quick tool to feel lighter, calmer, and happier throughout your day.

title: How Much Energy Does the Brain Use?
content:
Your brain uses a lot of energy to work well. Even when you’re resting, it needs constant fuel to send and receive information. Experts say the brain uses about 20% of the body’s total energy, making it one of the most energy-demanding organs.

Why the brain needs so much energy

The brain’s main job is communication. Neurons send electrical signals through tiny gaps called synapses. At these synapses, the brain uses energy to move ions in and out of cells, creating the electrical charge needed for signaling. Most of the brain’s energy goes into this process.

Which areas use more energy?

Gray matter uses far more energy than white matter because it contains synapses, cell bodies, and dendrites. White matter is mostly insulated axons, which use less energy.

Some brain functions also need more energy. For example, hearing requires fast, precise signals, so auditory areas use more energy than areas for smell or memory.

Does thinking hard use more energy?

The brain is always active, even during sleep. Your baseline brain energy stays high at all times. When you focus on a task, the energy in that specific brain area increases, but only by about 8%. This rise is small compared to how much energy muscles use when you exercise.

The myth that “you only use 10% of your brain” is false. Most neurons stay quiet until needed to save energy. If too many were active at once, the brain’s energy demand would skyrocket.

How energy needs shaped evolution

The brain must receive oxygen and energy constantly because it cannot store backup fuel. When blood flow stops, neurons shut down quickly, like during a stroke. This may seem like a weakness, but it evolved to keep the brain efficient. Storing extra energy inside the brain would take up space, slow communication, and require even more energy. Over time, evolution favored a fast, efficient system—even if it made the brain more vulnerable to injury.
author: Michael W. Richardson

title: Fitness & Nutrition Tips Just for Men
header: Discover Why Your Brain Uses So Much Energy Even When You Rest
content:
Many men don’t think about their health until something goes wrong. But simple daily habits can protect your long-term health and lower your risk of chronic diseases.

When you take care of yourself, you have more energy, feel better, and live a higher-quality life.

Core habits for a healthy man

  • Balanced hormones
  • Regular physical activity
  • Nutritious eating
  • Strong heart health

1. Support healthy testosterone

Testosterone affects muscle, energy, libido, bone strength and more. Levels naturally decline after 30, but unhealthy habits can lower them further.

Common causes of low testosterone include excess belly fat, inactivity, poor diet, high alcohol use, sleep apnea and unmanaged diabetes.

2. Stay physically active

Exercise helps with weight control, heart health, stronger muscles and bones, lower disease risk, better mood and longer life. Aim for at least 150 minutes per week. Resistance training is especially good for reducing belly fat and supporting testosterone.

3. Eat enough protein

Protein supports muscle, tissue repair and overall strength. Most men do well with 20–40g of protein per meal. Choose lean sources like poultry, fish, dairy, tofu, beans, nuts and whole grains.

4. Maintain a healthy weight

Belly fat (visceral fat) raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes. A balanced diet plus regular exercise helps reduce waist size. A Mediterranean-style eating pattern works well.

5. Know your body type

Ectomorphs are naturally slim, mesomorphs naturally muscular, and endomorphs gain weight more easily. Understanding your type helps set realistic fitness goals and avoid unfair comparisons.

6. Limit added sugars and refined carbs

Too much sugar lowers testosterone, increases weight gain and raises the risk of chronic illness. Men should limit added sugar to 36g per day. Watch out for hidden sugars in drinks, cereals, condiments and dressings.

7. Reduce sedentary habits

Sitting too much increases risks of obesity, high blood pressure and diabetes. Take movement breaks, stretch, walk, use stairs and reduce screen time.

8. Drink enough water and manage alcohol

Water supports heart, digestion, temperature control and muscle function. Men should aim for about 13 cups per day (adjust for activity and health). Drink alcohol responsibly.

9. Eat more fiber

Most men don’t get enough fiber. Aim for 25–38g daily. Good sources include whole grains, veggies, fruits, nuts and seeds.

10. Remove barriers to exercise

If time, motivation or weather get in the way, keep a small plan: pack workout clothes, create playlists, walk or jog, use bodyweight exercises or simple home equipment.

11. Get essential vitamins and minerals

Magnesium and zinc support testosterone, hair growth, muscle function and immunity. Good sources include seeds, nuts, beans, leafy greens, whole grains and lean meats.

12. Manage stress

Chronic stress raises cortisol, which increases belly fat and lowers testosterone. Use hobbies, movement, stretching, meditation or evening wind-down routines to restore balance.

13. Do pelvic floor exercises

Kegels help men maintain urinary control and can improve bladder issues and sexual function.

14. Choose healthy fats

Healthy unsaturated fats support hormone production. Good sources include avocados, olive oil, salmon, nuts and seeds.

15. Get your annual checkup

Regular exams help catch problems early. Your doctor will check vitals, run labs, screen for heart and metabolic issues, and review your mental health.

title: Reasons The Brain Loves Learning
header: Find Out How Learning Keeps Your Brain Sharp and Stress Low
content:
We often think learning only happens in school or work, but our brain learns something new every day. It’s built to seek new information and loves fresh skills, hobbies, and challenges. Here are three simple reasons why learning helps keep our brain happy and healthy.

1. Learning gives the brain a workout

Our brain runs many automatic tasks each day, and about 40% of what we do becomes habit. Habits save energy, but they don’t challenge the brain.

Learning something new creates fresh neural pathways. This process, called neuroplasticity, keeps the brain flexible, sharp, and healthy as we age. Every new skill, hobby, or idea strengthens your brain the same way exercise strengthens muscles.

2. Learning helps manage stress

Stress activates the fight-or-flight system, but our brain sometimes reacts too strongly to normal challenges, like taking a test.

By practicing new skills in stressful situations, we train the brain to calm down more easily. Over time, the amygdala (the stress center) becomes less reactive, lowering cortisol and making stress more manageable.

Learning doesn’t only build knowledge—it also teaches your brain to stay steady under pressure.

3. Curiosity is part of human evolution

Our brain loves novelty. Curiosity activates the reward system in the same way food and pleasure do, pushing us to explore, discover, and grow.

Asking questions sparks curiosity and activates the brain’s reticular activating system (RAS), which helps us notice information that matters. This makes learning easier and more enjoyable.

Small things—trying a new study method, learning in a new place, or exploring new hobbies—give your brain the novelty it craves.

Conclusion

Your brain is wired to learn. By keeping learning fun, fresh, and curiosity-driven, you build stronger neural pathways, better stress control, and endless personal growth. Keep exploring—your brain loves it.
author: Jim Kwik

title: How Gratitude Changes You and Your Brain
header: Learn Why Reflecting on Kindness Strengthens Emotional Resilience
content:
New research is showing that gratitude can meaningfully improve our mental health. Even simple gratitude practices, like writing a short letter of thanks, can make counseling more effective and help people feel better over time.

In one study of almost 300 adults seeking mental health support, participants were placed into three groups: one wrote a gratitude letter each week, one wrote about negative experiences, and one only received counseling. Those who wrote gratitude letters reported better mental health four and twelve weeks later — showing that gratitude works even for people struggling with anxiety or depression.

1. Gratitude helps release toxic emotions

People who wrote gratitude letters used fewer negative emotion words. This mattered more than using positive words. Writing about gratitude shifts attention away from resentment, anger, and rumination, giving the mind some relief.

2. Gratitude works even if you don’t send the letter

Only a small number of people actually sent their gratitude letters, yet most still benefited. This shows that simply writing the letter — reflecting on kindness and support — is enough to boost well-being.

3. Gratitude’s benefits grow over time

People didn’t feel better right away. But after a few weeks, the gratitude group showed clear improvements, and these effects became even stronger by 12 weeks. Gratitude creates a slow “snowball effect,” building emotional resilience with time.

4. Gratitude can change the brain

Three months after the writing exercise, brain scans showed that people who wrote gratitude letters had stronger activity in the medial prefrontal cortex — an area linked to learning, decision-making, and emotional regulation. This suggests gratitude can train the brain to notice positive experiences more easily.

Why this matters

Gratitude is simple, free, and can be added to regular counseling or personal routines. You don’t need perfect mental health to benefit. Even writing one short letter can start shifting attention away from negativity and toward appreciation.

Try it yourself

If you’ve never written a gratitude letter, try writing one to someone who has helped you. You don’t even have to send it. The act of writing alone can help reverse the habit of focusing on what’s missing — and help you notice what’s already good in your life.

title: Flexitarian Diet: Here's How It Can Improve Your Health

Health Benefits of a Flexitarian Diet

title: What percentage of our brain do we use?
header: Unlock Surprising Facts About How Your Brain Stays Active
content:
The brain is the most complex organ in the body. Many people believe we only use 10% of it, but research shows this is a myth. Most of the brain is active almost all the time, even when we are resting or sleeping.

How much of our brain do we use?

Studies using brain scans (like fMRI) show that simple actions require many brain areas to work. The amount of activity changes depending on what a person is doing, but we use far more than 10%.

Where the myth started

The 10% idea may have come from early psychology writings, misquoted books, or the fact that neurons make up about 10% of brain cells. Over time, movies and media helped spread the myth.

How to improve brain health

You can support your brain through lifestyle habits:

1. Eat a balanced diet

  • Dark fruits and vegetables (rich in vitamin E and beta carotene)
  • Oily fish like salmon and tuna (omega-3s)
  • Walnuts and pecans (antioxidants)

2. Exercise regularly

Cardio activities such as walking, biking, jogging, or swimming help reduce conditions that can lead to memory decline.

3. Keep the brain active

Brain exercises improve processing speed and reduce dementia risk. Learning new skills keeps the brain strong.

Other common brain myths

Left brain vs. right brain

You are not “left-brained” or “right-brained.” Both sides work together all the time.

Alcohol kills brain cells

Alcohol misuse can harm the brain, but it doesn’t simply “kill” brain cells. Effects are more complex.

Subliminal learning

You cannot learn brand-new information while asleep, but you may strengthen memories you learned earlier.

Brain wrinkles

Wrinkles form before birth and help increase brain surface area. Learning does not create new wrinkles, but it does create new connections.

Interesting brain facts

  • The brain is 2% of your body weight but uses 20% of your oxygen and calories.
  • The brain is about 73% water; even mild dehydration affects memory and focus.
  • About 25% of the body's cholesterol is in the brain, and it is essential for brain cell health.

Takeaway

The idea that we use only 10% of our brain is false. Almost all of the brain is active, even during simple tasks. Scientists continue to discover how this powerful organ works, separating myths from facts.

title: Discouragement and failures are two of the surest stepping stones to success.
header: Find Out Why Reflecting on Mistakes Boosts Growth and Confidence
content:
"Develop success from failures. Discouragement and failures are two of the surest stepping stones to success." – Dale Carnegie

Take a moment to look back at your past week. Where did you fail? Where did you fall short of your expectations?

When we reflect on our failures, we often discover lessons and areas for growth. Maybe there was a conversation where you thought, "I wish I had said this," or a meeting that needed more preparation. Maybe you tried a new approach at work or created a new idea for your class.

The truth is, we all fail at something every day. Each day offers small moments and situations that help us improve. But growth requires intention. We need the mindset to reflect, learn, and keep moving forward.

This mindset protects us from discouragement. Even more, it becomes a source of encouragement — because every failure becomes a stepping stone toward success.

title: Why staying happy means staying busy
header: Explore How Small Tasks With Meaning Improve Well-Being
content:
People stay busy for many reasons — to earn money, gain recognition, improve society, protect themselves, or simply feel productive. But research suggests something deeper: we dislike idleness, yet we also want a reason to stay active.

Studies from NUS, the University of Chicago, and Shanghai Jiaotong University show that people are happier when busy — even if the task is small or the reason is weak — as long as it feels justifiable.

For example, airports make passengers walk farther to baggage claim to reduce idle waiting time. Experiments also showed that volunteers were happier choosing a longer walk or a simple task when they had even a small reason to justify being active.

Why this happens

Humans prefer purposeful action. Evolution likely taught us that wasting energy without reason could harm survival. So while being busy makes us feel good, we avoid activity that seems pointless.

Constructive vs. destructive busyness

Busyness can improve life — or harm it. When people lack purpose, idleness can lead to destructive behavior. As technology and automation reduce the need to work, we will have more free time than ever, making purposeful busyness even more important.

The key idea

We often say we work hard so we can rest, but research suggests the opposite may also be true: we stay active to avoid the unhappiness that comes with idleness. Time feels empty when we are idle; it feels meaningful when used toward a purpose — even a small one.

title: Maintain balance with a healthy lifestyle
header: Learn How Lifestyle Changes Can Strengthen Your Stress Coping Skills
content:
Along with regular exercise, healthy lifestyle habits can strengthen your ability to cope with stress.

Eat a healthy diet. A well-nourished body handles stress better. Start your day with breakfast and choose balanced, nutritious meals to keep your energy steady and your mind clear.

Reduce caffeine and sugar. The quick “high” from caffeine and sugar often ends in a crash. Cutting back on coffee, soft drinks, chocolate, and sugary snacks can help you feel calmer and improve sleep.

Avoid alcohol, cigarettes, and drugs. These may offer temporary relief, but they don’t solve the problem. Facing challenges with a clear mind is healthier and more effective.

Get enough sleep. Good sleep restores both body and mind. When you're tired, stress increases and clear thinking becomes harder.

title: Smiling Really Is Contagious, And Here's Why
header: Find Out Why Seeing a Facial Expression Changes Your Mood
content:
When you smile at someone, more happens than you realize. Research shows that all facial expressions are contagious because our brains tend to mimic what we see.

This process, called sensorimotor simulation, helps us understand other people's emotions. When you see someone smile or frown, your brain automatically recreates that expression, helping you interpret how they feel.

After reviewing over 120 studies, researchers found that mimicking a facial expression can trigger the same emotional state in us. This helps us respond appropriately in social situations.

Eye contact is one of the easiest ways to activate this mimicry. Looking into someone’s eyes helps you understand them better — and helps them understand you.

Facial mimicry also influences social decisions. Your emotional reaction shapes how you perceive another person’s expression and whether you move toward them or avoid them.

However, facial expressions are complex. Experts note that mimicry alone can’t explain every emotional interaction, and conditions like facial paralysis or autism can affect one’s ability to mimic or read emotions.

Understanding how humans quickly interpret subtle facial signals may help improve social and emotional support for people who struggle with emotion recognition.
author: Jacqueline Howard

title: Why You Should Reduce Excessive Salt Intake & How To
header: Discover How Too Much Salt Harms Your Heart, Brain, and Bones
content:
Salt is a mineral made of sodium and chloride. While the body needs small amounts, eating too much salt can harm your health. Below are the major ways excessive salt affects the body and simple tips to reduce your intake.

Why reducing salt matters:

1. High blood pressure

Too much salt raises blood pressure, increasing the risk of heart disease, stroke, and kidney issues.

2. Heart problems

Excess salt stiffens and narrows blood vessels, raising the risk of heart attacks and other heart conditions.

3. Fluid retention

High salt causes the body to hold extra water, leading to swelling, bloating, and temporary weight gain.

4. Kidney strain

Extra salt forces the kidneys to work harder and can lead to kidney stones and long-term kidney damage.

5. Bone weakness

A high-salt diet causes the body to lose calcium, increasing the risk of low bone density and osteoporosis.

6. Stomach cancer risk

Too much salt can damage the stomach lining and support harmful bacteria, increasing stomach cancer risk.

7. Cognitive decline

Research shows high salt intake may affect memory, focus, and overall brain function.

8. Dehydration

Salt upsets the body’s fluid balance, causing dehydration, tiredness, and dizziness.

9. Autoimmune issues

Some studies suggest excess salt may influence autoimmune diseases like MS or rheumatoid arthritis.

10. Mental health impact

High salt intake has been linked to higher risks of anxiety and depression.

How to reduce your salt intake:

  • Choose low-sodium or no-added-salt packaged foods.
  • Cook more meals at home using fresh ingredients.
  • Use herbs, spices, garlic, or lemon for flavour instead of salt.
  • Cut back on processed and fast foods.
  • Pick low-sodium canned foods and condiments.
  • Request less salt when dining out.
  • Stay hydrated throughout the day.
  • Eat more fruits and vegetables.
  • Choose healthier snacks like nuts, fruit, or plain popcorn instead of salty chips.

If needed, speak with a dietitian or healthcare provider for personal advice.

title: Protect your brain from stress
header: Learn How Managing Stress Supports Brain Health and Cognitive Function
content:
Stress management can help reduce health problems linked to stress, including cognitive decline, Alzheimer's disease, and dementia.

Feeling disorganized or forgetful during stressful times is common. But long-term stress can actually change the brain in ways that affect memory, focus, and thinking.

Research in both humans and animals shows that stress interferes with cognition, attention, and memory. Stress also promotes inflammation, which affects heart health and may contribute to chronic diseases.

How stress affects the brain

The brain is made of different parts that perform different tasks. When you face danger or intense emotions, the amygdala (the brain’s survival center) becomes highly active. This takes energy away from brain areas responsible for memory and higher-level thinking. As a result, you may become forgetful or struggle to concentrate.

Stress may also affect the brain differently depending on life stages. Hormonal changes during puberty, pregnancy, or menopause can influence how the brain responds to stress.

How to protect your brain from damaging stress

These strategies can help reduce stress and protect your cognitive health:

  • Establish control where you can. Routines help the brain feel safe and predictable, which reduces stress.
  • Prioritize good sleep. Stress disrupts sleep, and poor sleep weakens the brain’s ability to think clearly. Go to bed at the same time daily, avoid caffeine after noon, and create a calm sleep environment.
  • Get organized. Break tasks into a simple daily list so your brain feels less overloaded. Knowing exactly what needs to be done helps reduce stress.
  • Get help when needed. Support from others builds resilience and may prevent long-term effects of stress.
  • Shift your mindset. Some stress is normal and can even help growth. Instead of avoiding stress completely, focus on responding to it in healthier ways.

How long-term stress changes the brain

Chronic stress can “rewire” the brain. It strengthens the survival-focused areas (like the amygdala) and weakens areas responsible for planning, memory, and decision-making (like the prefrontal cortex). This shift makes it harder to think clearly when stress is ongoing.

Some changes may be reversible, especially when stress decreases or coping strategies improve. In some cases—especially after childhood stress—people may develop new brain pathways that help them become more resilient.

Is all stress equally harmful?

Not all stress affects the brain the same way. Intense, long-lasting, or unpredictable stress tends to be more damaging. Stress becomes especially harmful when:

  • The stress is unpredictable. The brain handles stress better when it can anticipate it.
  • The stress has no clear end. Ongoing stress—like chronic financial worries—can be harder to manage.
  • There is little or no support. Feeling alone during stressful times increases emotional and cognitive strain.

While stress is a normal part of life, managing it well can protect your brain, improve memory, and support long-term health.
